title: Six leaks
hook: wealth drains through drink, night-roaming, fairs, gambling, bad company and idleness
carry: too hot, too late, too tired

segments.voice: Yesterday: four motives, desire, hate, delusion and fear. Your line: desire, hate, delusion, or fear? Today the Buddha talks to Sigala about money.

Open a banking app and look at last month. There's usually no single disaster. Just a lot of small drips: a subscription you forgot, takeout three nights running, a late-night purchase you can't quite remember making. The money didn't explode. It leaked. The Buddha, talking to a young householder in a world with no apps, names the same thing: six openings through which a household's wealth drains away.
screen: `NO DISASTER, JUST DRIPS.` → `A YOUNG HOUSEHOLDER'S BUDGET.` → `SIX OPENINGS.`

segments.voice: The Pali word is apayamukha, literally a mouth or opening toward loss. The six: drinking intoxicants, roaming the streets at the wrong hours, haunting fairs and shows, gambling, keeping bad company, and idleness. For each one, the Buddha lists six dangers, and the details are wonderfully specific. Gambling: the winner makes enemies, the loser mourns what he lost, his money is gone, his word isn't trusted when he speaks in public, his friends look down on him, and nobody wants him to marry into their family. Roaming at night: he leaves himself unprotected, and his family and property too, he's suspected of crimes, and rumors attach to him. And idleness has the best list of all. The idle man doesn't work, saying: it's too cold. It's too hot. It's too late. It's too early. I'm too hungry. I'm too full. Every reason sounds reasonable. That's what makes it a leak. This isn't a sermon against pleasure, and he isn't asking a householder to live like a monk. Elsewhere in the same sutta he tells him to enjoy part of his wealth. He's simply pointing to where it goes when you're not watching. And the leaks aren't only money. Each one drains time, health, trust and friendships too. None of them is dramatic. It's one more drink, one more night out, one more too late, too early.
screen: `APAYAMUKHA: OPENINGS TO LOSS.` · `SIX LEAKS, SIX DANGERS EACH.` · `TOO COLD, TOO HOT, TOO LATE.` · `NOT A SERMON AGAINST PLEASURE.` · then, large: `SIX LEAKS.`

segments.voice: Look honestly at your own week, without blame, and ask where something leaks: money, yes, but also time, energy, attention. Let the most ordinary leak come to mind, and picture the moment it usually happens: the evening, the phone, the excuse. Breathe with it, and picture plugging it, just once.
Six leaks. In DN 31 the six openings through which wealth drains: drink, night-roaming, fairs, gambling, bad company and idleness. Today's word.
Your line: too hot, too late, too tired. Small drips, not disasters. Day five hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often teach the Sigalovada's six leaks to lay people as practical household advice, and Buddhist economics writers cite it alongside the sutta's advice on saving and sharing wealth.

fork.setup: it's a hot afternoon and there's work to do. the idle man in the Sigalovada has an answer ready. what is it?
options: I'll do twice as much tomorrow.
fork.reveal: it's too hot, and if it isn't, it's too cold, too late, too early, too hungry or too full.

original.note: Pali apayamukha: apaya, loss or ruin; mukha, mouth or opening. the six leaks of DN 31.

trapdoor: what you thought: wealth is lost in big disasters.
what it means: in DN 31 it drains through six ordinary openings, each with its own six dangers.
what a scholar hears: the Sigalovada's apayamukha list, with sixfold dangers for each, is among the most practical economic passages in the Pali canon.

chat.says: Did the Buddha think spending money on fun was wrong?
options: No; he told Sigala to enjoy part of his wealth, and to watch for six leaks.
Yes; he wanted every householder to give all their money away.
No; he only warned against gambling, and everything else was fine.
chat.meaning: In DN 31 the Buddha names six openings to loss, like gambling and idleness, but isn't against pleasure: he tells Sigala to enjoy part of his wealth.

apayamukha.meaning: an opening toward loss, a leak

Sigala.meaning: a young householder the Buddha advised

sutta.meaning: a discourse, a teaching of the Buddha

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 31 (Sigalovada Sutta), the six channels for dissipating wealth
